entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret $e^{st}$ as the generalized continuous-time exponential form that unifies real exponentials, complex exponentials, and the damped or growing sinusoidal signals developed next.

sections.section_title: Introduction to The Generalized Exponential Signal $e^{st}$

blocks.text: Read $x(t)=e^{st}$ as a continuous-time signal in the variable $t$, with $s$ held fixed as the parameter that sets the signal’s behavior.
When $s$ is fixed, the formula no longer names a general algebraic expression. It names one specific signal in time, and changing the value of $s$ changes which signal you get.
Start with the simple real choice $s=-1$. Then the same form becomes the familiar decaying exponential $x(t)=e^{-t}$, which is the cleanest base case for this module.

This is why $e^{st}$ is called the generalized exponential signal: the same template will later cover real exponentials first, then complex choices of $s$, and then the damped or growing sinusoidal cases that follow.
For now, keep the roles separate: $t$ is the variable, $s$ is the fixed parameter, and $e^{st}$ is the signal form that ties the later special cases together.

sections.section_title: Reading $e^{st}$ as a Continuous-Time Signal with Fixed $s$

example_content.example_prompt: Let $s=-2+j3$. Write the corresponding signal as $x(t)=e^{st}$ and explain what stays fixed and what changes with time.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a fixed complex value of $s$. Once $s$ is fixed, $x(t)=e^{st}$ names one specific continuous-time signal in $t$, not a formula with two variables competing for the same role.
Substitute the fixed parameter directly into the exponent: $s=-2+j3$ becomes $x(t)=e^{(-2+j3)t}$. The parameter stays fixed, and $t$ is the variable that traces the signal over time.

So the notation $x(t)=e^{st}$ means a concrete time signal once $s$ is chosen. This is the same generalized exponential form from the previous step, now read with one fixed parameter value instead of left abstract.

sections.section_title: Matching Real Values of $s$ to Real Exponential Signals

example_content.example_prompt: Let $s=-3$. Match this value to the corresponding signal and classify it as growing, decaying, or constant.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is a real value of $s$. Once $s$ is fixed and real, $x(t)=e^{st}$ is a pure real exponential signal in $t$, and the sign of $s$ determines whether it grows, decays, or stays constant.
Substitute $s=-3$ into $x(t)=e^{st}$ to get $x(t)=e^{-3t}$. The parameter is fixed, and $t$ is the variable that traces the signal over time.
The negative coefficient means the signal decays as $t$ increases, so the matching classification is decaying. If $s=0$, the same form would become $x(t)=e^{0t}=1$, which is the constant case.

sections.section_title: Matching Pure Imaginary Values of $s$ to Complex Exponential Signals

example_content.example_prompt: Let $s=j4$. Match this value to the corresponding signal and interpret the result as a pure complex exponential.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is a pure imaginary value of $s$. When $s$ has no real part, $x(t)=e^{st}$ becomes a complex exponential with constant magnitude and oscillatory phase rather than growth or decay.
Substitute $s=j4$ into $x(t)=e^{st}$ to get $x(t)=e^{j4t}$. The parameter stays fixed, and $t$ is the variable that traces the oscillation over time.
So $s=j4$ matches the pure complex exponential $x(t)=e^{j4t}$. In Euler-style language, this is a constant-magnitude oscillation with no exponential growth or decay.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Complex Values of $s$ as Combined Exponential and Oscillatory Behavior

example_content.example_prompt: Let $s=-2+j5$. Separate $x(t)=e^{st}$ into envelope and oscillation factors and describe the resulting behavior.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a complex value of $s$ with both a real part and an imaginary part. Write $s=\sigma+j\omega$ so the real part sets the envelope rate and the imaginary part sets the oscillation rate.
Substitute $s=-2+j5$ into $x(t)=e^{st}$ and separate the result into the real-part factor and the imaginary-part factor. In general, $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}=e^{\sigma t}e^{j\omega t}$.
Here $e^{-2t}$ is the envelope and $e^{j5t}$ is the oscillation. Because the real part is negative, the envelope decays, so $s=-2+j5$ gives a damped complex exponential.

entries.lesson_core_move: Decompose $s=\sigma+j\omega$ in $e^{st}=e^{\sigma t}e^{j\omega t}$ to identify $\sigma$ as the growth-or-decay envelope rate and $\omega$ as the oscillation rate of a generalized exponential signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Real and Imaginary Parts of $s=\sigma+j\omega$

blocks.text: For generalized exponential signals, treat $t$ as the variable and $s$ as a fixed parameter. Write the signal as $x(t)=e^{st}$ so the same form can name a whole family of continuous-time signals.

If you hold $s$ fixed, the formula becomes one specific signal in $t$. A simple real choice such as $s=-1$ gives $x(t)=e^{-t}$, a plain decaying exponential that anchors the notation before any more complicated choices of $s$ appear.

This is the reading rule for the rest of the module: one fixed value of $s$ selects one signal, and the same exponential form can later produce other special cases. In the next section, you will use one concrete value of $s$ and read the corresponding signal directly.

example_content.example_prompt: For $s=-3+j4$, identify $\sigma$ and $\omega$.

explanation_blocks.text: Read $s=-3+j4$ in the standard form $s=\sigma+j\omega$. The real part is the number without $j$, and the imaginary part is the coefficient of $j$.
So $\sigma=-3$ and $\omega=4$. This is the direct read-off rule: match the real part to $\sigma$ and the coefficient of $j$ to $\omega$.
In $e^{st}$, that means the envelope decays while the signal oscillates at rate $4$. The sign of $\sigma$ controls the decay or growth, and $\omega$ controls the oscillation rate.

sections.section_title: Factoring $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ into Envelope and Oscillation Parts

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $e^{(-2+j5)t}$ as a product of an envelope factor and an oscillation factor, then identify each factor.

explanation_blocks.text: Start with the cue $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$. Here the exponent is $(-2+j5)t$, so the first step is to distribute $t$ across the real and imaginary parts.
That becomes $e^{-2t+j5t}$. Now use $e^{a+b}=e^ae^b$ to split the signal into separate factors.
So the envelope factor is $e^{-2t}$ and the oscillation factor is $e^{j5t}$. The real part $-2$ sets the decay rate, and the imaginary part $5$ sets the oscillation rate.

sections.section_title: Interpreting $\sigma$ as the Growth or Decay Rate

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{(-4+j2)t}$, determine whether the envelope grows or decays and state the rate set by $\sigma$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the real part of the exponent in $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$. Here $s=-4+j2$, so $\sigma=-4$.
The envelope factor is $e^{-4t}$. Because the exponent is negative, the envelope decreases as $t$ increases, so the signal decays rather than grows.
So $\sigma=-4$ means decay at rate $4$. The oscillatory factor $e^{j2t}$ stays separate and does not change the envelope interpretation.

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{(-1+j6)t}$, identify $\omega$ and explain how it sets the oscillation rate.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the imaginary part of the exponent in $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$. Here $s=-1+j6$, so $\omega=6$.
The envelope factor $e^{-t}$ stays separate. The oscillatory factor is $e^{j6t}$, and $|\omega|=6$ sets the oscillation rate, so a larger $|\omega|$ means faster oscillation.
So $\omega=6$ means oscillation at rate $6$. The sign of $\omega$ changes direction, but the magnitude controls how fast the oscillation varies, while $\sigma$ still controls the envelope.

sections.section_title: Reading Both Rates from a Generalized Exponential Signal

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{(2-j3)t}$, read off $\sigma$ and $\omega$ and state the envelope and oscillation behavior of the signal.

explanation_blocks.text: Read the real and imaginary parts of $s=2-j3$ together: $\sigma=2$ and $\omega=-3$.
The factor $e^{2t}$ is the envelope, so the signal grows. The factor $e^{-j3t}$ is the oscillation, and $|\omega|=3$ sets its rate.
So the complete description is growth at rate $2$ and oscillation at rate $3$. This is the full envelope-and-oscillation reading of a generalized exponential signal.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret pure real exponentials by setting $s=\sigma$ in $e^{st}$ and using the sign and magnitude of $\sigma$ to determine non-oscillatory growth, decay, or constancy over time.

blocks.text: Set $s=\sigma$ in the generalized exponential $e^{st}$ and you get the pure real exponential $x(t)=e^{\sigma t}$. Here $t$ is the variable and $\sigma$ is a fixed real number, so the only thing the signal can do is change in magnitude over time.
Use $\sigma=0$ as the base case. Then $e^{0t}=1$, which is the constant unit signal and the cleanest reference point for the sign rule.
When $\sigma<0$, the signal decays toward $0$ as $t$ increases. When $\sigma>0$, it grows. In both cases the behavior is non-oscillatory because the exponent is real.
The size of $|\sigma|$ controls how fast the change happens: larger $|\sigma|$ means faster decay or faster growth. That sign-and-magnitude rule is the core way to read pure real exponentials.

example_content.example_prompt: Let $s=-4$ in $e^{st}$. Rewrite the signal and identify whether it grows, decays, or stays constant.

explanation_blocks.text: Because $s$ is real, write $s=\sigma$ with $\sigma=-4$. Substituting that value into $e^{st}$ gives the pure real exponential form in $t$.
Since $\sigma=-4<0$, the exponent becomes more negative as $t$ increases, so the signal decays toward $0$. There is no oscillation here because the exponent is real.
The magnitude $|\sigma|=4$ controls how fast the decay happens, but the sign is what tells you that this signal decays rather than grows or stays constant.

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{-2t}$, describe the behavior as $t$ increases and explain why the exponent sign forces decay.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a real coefficient, so write $s=\sigma$. Here $\sigma=-2<0$, which puts the signal in the decay case right away.
Substituting gives $x(t)=e^{-2t}$. As $t$ increases, the exponent becomes more negative, so the signal shrinks toward $0$.
Because the exponent is real, there is no oscillation. The sign tells you it decays, and the magnitude $|\sigma|=2$ sets how fast it decays.

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{3t}$, describe the behavior as $t$ increases and explain why the positive exponent forces growth.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a real coefficient, so write $s=\sigma$. Here $\sigma=3>0$, which puts the signal in the growth case right away.
Substituting gives $x(t)=e^{3t}$. As $t$ increases, the exponent becomes more positive, so the signal increases without bound and never oscillates.
Because the exponent is real, the rise is monotone rather than oscillatory. The sign tells you it grows, and the magnitude $|\sigma|=3$ sets how fast it grows.

example_content.example_prompt: Set $\sigma=0$ in $e^{\sigma t}$ and determine the resulting signal.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a real coefficient, so write $s=\sigma$. Here $\sigma=0$, which is the boundary case between growth and decay.
Substituting gives $x(t)=e^{0t}=1$. The value no longer depends on $t$, so the signal stays constant at the unit level.
Because the exponent is real and equal to zero, there is no oscillation and no growth or decay. The zero exponent produces the constant unit signal.

example_content.example_prompt: Compare $x(t)=e^{-2t}$ and $y(t)=e^{-5t}$ and decide which one decays faster.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both exponents are real and negative, so both signals are in the decay case. To compare their rates, look at the magnitudes $|\sigma|$.
Here $|{-5}|>|{-2}|$, so $y(t)$ has the larger magnitude exponent. That means $y(t)$ changes faster in magnitude, so it decays faster than $x(t)$ as $t$ increases.

The general rule is that the sign tells you whether the signal grows or decays, while the larger $|\sigma|$ tells you which one changes faster. In this case, both signals decay, and the one with the larger magnitude decays more quickly.

entries.lesson_core_move: Convert $e^{st}$ with $s=j\omega$ into $e^{j\omega t}=\cos(\omega t)+j\sin(\omega t)$ to interpret pure complex exponentials as constant-magnitude rotating phasors rather than growing or decaying signals.

blocks.text: Generalized exponential signals use $e^{st}$. Here $s$ can carry both growth or decay and oscillation.

In the pure complex case, set $s=j\omega$. The real part is zero, so the exponential envelope disappears. Use the concrete base case $e^{jt}$ first so the learner sees a unit-magnitude rotating signal before returning to general $\omega$.
Now apply Euler's formula to rewrite the signal in rectangular form.
This rewrite is a point on the unit circle: the cosine gives the real part, the sine gives the imaginary part, and the angle changes with time while the magnitude stays fixed.
So $e^{j\omega t}$ is the pure complex exponential case: it rotates like a phasor, but it does not grow or decay.

example_content.example_prompt: Starting from $e^{st}$, substitute $s=j\omega$ and rewrite the signal.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the generalized exponential $e^{st}$ with a fixed complex exponent. Here the move is to set $s=j\omega$.
That substitution locks the real part of $s$ at zero, so the growth-or-decay envelope disappears and only the oscillatory part remains.
So the signal becomes $e^{j\omega t}$. It is still oscillatory, but it is no longer growing or decaying.

example_content.example_prompt: Expand $e^{j\omega t}$ using Euler's formula and identify its real and imaginary parts.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the pure complex exponential $e^{j\omega t}$. To expose its structure, rewrite it with Euler's formula.
From this form, the real part is $\cos(\omega t)$ and the imaginary part is $\sin(\omega t)$.
That is the direct cosine-sine decomposition of $e^{j\omega t}$, and it is the form you will reuse in the next step.

sections.section_title: Interpreting $e^{j\omega t}$ as a Rotating Phasor

image_slots.image_description: Textbook-style line art on a white background: draw the complex plane with a labeled real axis and imaginary axis, a unit circle centered at the origin, and a bold phasor arrow from the origin to a point on the circle at angle $\omega t$ measured counterclockwise from the positive real axis. Label the angle arc $\omega t$ and keep the arrow length equal to 1. Optionally include a faint second arrow or trail showing an earlier position to suggest counterclockwise rotation as $t$ increases when $\omega>0$.

example_content.example_prompt: Use the complex-plane picture to explain how $e^{j\omega t}$ traces a rotating phasor.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the pair $\cos(\omega t)$ and $\sin(\omega t)$ from the Euler expansion. Put that pair on the complex plane as a point.
The point stays on the unit circle because its magnitude is $1$. Its angle from the positive real axis is $\omega t$.
For $\omega>0$, increasing $t$ moves the point counterclockwise. That moving unit-length vector is the phasor interpretation of $e^{j\omega t}$.

sections.section_title: Recognizing Constant Magnitude Instead of Growth or Decay

example_content.example_prompt: Compare $e^{j\omega t}$ with $e^{\sigma t}$ and decide whether the signal grows, decays, or stays at constant magnitude.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the exponent: $e^{j\omega t}$ has real part $0$. Only a nonzero real part creates the envelope $e^{\sigma t}$ that makes a signal grow or decay.
Because $\sigma=0$, the magnitude stays at $1$ for all $t$. There is no growth and no decay.
So the correct classification is constant magnitude. Pure complex exponentials are the zero-growth, zero-decay case.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ with $\sigma<0$ as a damped sinusoid by separating the decaying envelope $e^{\sigma t}$ from the oscillatory factor $e^{j\omega t}$ and identifying the resulting amplitude decay rate and angular frequency.

blocks.text: A damped sinusoid is a generalized exponential of the form $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ with $\sigma<0$. Read the real part $\sigma$ as the decay part and the imaginary part $\omega$ as the oscillation part.

The factor $e^{\sigma t}$ is the decaying envelope, and the factor $e^{j\omega t}$ is the oscillatory part. That split is the key move: one factor controls amplitude, and the other factor controls oscillation.
Because $\sigma<0$, the envelope gets smaller as $t$ increases, so the amplitude decays at rate $-\sigma$. The more negative $\sigma$ is, the faster that decay happens.

The oscillatory factor is still $e^{j\omega t}=\cos(\omega t)+j\sin(\omega t)$, so the angular frequency is $\omega$ rad/s. In short, $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ is a decaying oscillation whose amplitude falls like $e^{\sigma t}$.

sections.section_title: Separating a Damped Complex Exponential into Envelope and Oscillation

example_content.example_prompt: Work through $x(t)=e^{(-1.5+j4)t}$ by separating the envelope and oscillatory factor, then label the decay rate and angular frequency.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is the complex exponent $s=-1.5+j4$, so split the signal into its real and imaginary parts. The real part will give the decaying envelope, and the imaginary part will give the oscillation.
Now the first factor, $e^{-1.5t}$, is the envelope, and the second factor, $e^{j4t}$, is the oscillatory term. That is the only split you need for this step.
From the envelope, read the decay rate as $1.5$ and note that the amplitude shrinks exponentially with $t$. From the oscillatory factor, read the angular frequency as $4$ rad/s.
So $x(t)$ is a damped oscillation: it rotates at $4$ rad/s while its amplitude falls like $e^{-1.5t}$. The same split works whenever $s=\sigma+j\omega$ has a negative real part.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Decay Rate from Negative $\sigma$

example_content.example_prompt: Work through $x(t)=e^{(-3+j2)t}$ by reading the decay rate from the negative real part and explaining how the envelope changes over time.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the negative real part in $-3+j2$. Split the exponent so the decaying envelope and the oscillation are separate.

Here $e^{-3t}$ is the envelope and $e^{j2t}$ is the oscillatory factor. The decay rate is the magnitude of the negative real part, so the amplitude decays at rate $3$ per unit time. The $j2$ term still gives angular frequency $2$ rad/s; it does not change the decay rate.
Because $\sigma=-3$, the amplitude shrinks toward zero as $t$ increases. A more negative $\sigma$ would mean faster decay, while a less negative $\sigma$ would mean slower decay.

example_content.example_prompt: Work through $x(t)=e^{(-1+j6)t}$ by isolating the oscillatory factor and reading the angular frequency from the imaginary part.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the imaginary part in $-1+j6$. Keep the damping factor fixed and read the oscillation from the $j6$ term.
Here $e^{-t}$ is the envelope and $e^{j6t}$ is the oscillatory factor. The angular frequency is the coefficient of $t$ in the imaginary exponent, so $\omega=6$ rad/s.
Do not read frequency from the real part. The decay rate is $1$ per unit time, but the angular frequency is $6$ rad/s, so the signal oscillates at $6$ rad/s while its amplitude decays.

example_content.example_prompt: Work through $x(t)=e^{(-2+j4)t}$ by interpreting the full damped-sinusoid behavior directly from $s=\sigma+j\omega$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the full complex parameter $s=-2+j4$. Read the real and imaginary parts together: the real part controls decay, and the imaginary part controls oscillation.
Here $\sigma=-2$ and $\omega=4$. From $e^{-2t}$, the envelope decays at rate $2$ per unit time. From $e^{j4t}$, the angular frequency is $4$ rad/s.
So the signal is a damped sinusoid: it oscillates at $4$ rad/s while its amplitude shrinks toward zero. The real part sets damping, and the imaginary part sets frequency.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify growing sinusoids within $e^{st}$ by recognizing $\sigma>0$ in $s=\sigma+j\omega$, interpreting $e^{\sigma t}$ as the increasing envelope and $\omega$ as the oscillation rate.

blocks.text: Define $x(t)=e^{st}$ as a continuous-time signal with $s=\sigma+j\omega$ held fixed and $t$ as the variable. In this lesson, we isolate the case $\sigma>0$ so the same formula can be read as a growing sinusoid.

In the simple base case $s=1+j\omega$, the signal already splits into a real exponential factor and an oscillatory complex exponential factor. That is the pattern to keep in view before generalizing to arbitrary $\sigma>0$.
When $\sigma>0$, the factor $e^{\sigma t}$ increases with $t$, so it acts as the envelope of the signal. The factor $e^{j\omega t}$ supplies the oscillation.
That magnitude formula ties the envelope directly to the real part of $s$: $\sigma$ controls the growth, and $\omega$ controls the oscillation rate.
So the classification rule is simple: if $s=\sigma+j\omega$ and $\sigma>0$, then $e^{st}$ is a growing sinusoid with increasing envelope $e^{\sigma t}$ and oscillation rate $\omega$.

example_content.example_prompt: Classify $x(t)=e^{(2+j3)t}$ by identifying $\sigma$ and $\omega$ and deciding whether the signal grows, decays, or stays constant.

explanation_blocks.text: Start by reading the exponent in standard form. In $x(t)=e^{(2+j3)t}$, the fixed parameter is $s=2+j3$, so the cue is a positive real part.
Because $\sigma=2>0$, the real part is positive. That means the exponential factor is growing, not decaying or staying constant.
The factor $e^{2t}$ is the increasing envelope, and $e^{j3t}$ is the oscillatory factor. The number $3$ sets the oscillation rate, while $2$ sets the growth rate.
So the signal is a growing sinusoid: positive $\sigma$ gives growth, and $\omega$ still controls the oscillation rate.

example_content.example_prompt: Rewrite $e^{(1.5+j4)t}$ as a product and name which factor controls growth and which factor controls oscillation.

explanation_blocks.text: Start by reading the exponent in standard form. Here $s=1.5+j4$, so the cue is to split the real part from the imaginary part.
Now apply the split inside $e^{st}$. The real part becomes the growth factor $e^{\sigma t}$, and the imaginary part stays in the oscillatory factor $e^{j\omega t}$.
The factor $e^{1.5t}$ controls the increasing envelope because its magnitude grows with $t$. The factor $e^{j4t}$ controls the oscillation rate.
So the product form makes the roles explicit: $\sigma=1.5$ gives growth, and $\omega=4$ gives oscillation.

sections.section_title: Interpreting $e^{\sigma t}$ as an Increasing Envelope

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{0.5t}e^{j4t}$, identify the envelope and explain how it changes as $t$ increases.

explanation_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{0.5t}e^{j4t}$, match the real exponential factor $e^{\sigma t}$ to the envelope. Here that factor is $e^{0.5t}$.
Here $\sigma=0.5>0$, so the envelope is increasing rather than shrinking or staying constant.
As $t$ increases, $e^{0.5t}$ gets larger, so the oscillation keeps the same rate but rides inside a widening envelope.
So the envelope is $e^{0.5t}$, and the positive real part is exactly what makes it grow.

sections.section_title: Reading Growth Rate and Oscillation Rate Together

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{0.75t}e^{j8t}$, state the growth rate, the oscillation rate, and the overall classification.

explanation_blocks.text: Start by reading the exponent in standard form. The cue is that $s=0.75+j8$, so the real part gives growth and the imaginary part gives oscillation.
Since $\sigma=0.75>0$, the envelope is $e^{0.75t}$ and it increases with time.
So the growth rate is $0.75$, the oscillation rate is $8$, and the signal is a growing sinusoid with envelope $e^{0.75t}$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify the exponential envelope $e^{\sigma t}$ that bounds the oscillatory components of $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$ and use the sign of $\sigma$ to interpret damping, growth, or constant-amplitude behavior.

blocks.text: An exponential envelope is the real exponential factor $e^{\sigma t}$ inside $e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}$. It controls the size of the oscillation, while $e^{j\omega t}$ controls the oscillation itself.
Write the signal as $e^{\sigma t}e^{j\omega t}$. That split separates the amplitude envelope from the oscillatory factor you already know.
The envelope is the magnitude scale: $\left|e^{(\sigma+j\omega)t}\right|=e^{\sigma t}$. If you look at the real part, the oscillation stays between $-e^{\sigma t}$ and $e^{\sigma t}$.
The boundary case is $\sigma=0$, so $e^{\sigma t}=1$. In that case the envelope is flat and the signal keeps constant amplitude.
From the sign of $\sigma$, you will later read decay when $\sigma<0$ and growth when $\sigma>0$, using the same factorization each time.

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{(-3+j4)t}$, identify the exponential envelope and the oscillatory factor.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the mixed exponent $(-3+j4)t$. The real part $-3$ sets the amplitude envelope, and the imaginary part $j4$ gives the oscillation you already know.
Rewrite the signal as $e^{-3t}e^{j4t}$. That split isolates $e^{-3t}$ as the exponential envelope and leaves $e^{j4t}$ as the oscillatory factor.
So the envelope is $e^{-3t}$. That is the factor that later tells you whether the signal decays or grows from the sign of $\sigma$.

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{(-3+j4)t}$, explain how the envelope behaves as $t$ increases.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the negative real part $\sigma=-3$. That means the same factorization from the previous example will produce an envelope that shrinks as time increases.
Write $x(t)=e^{-3t}e^{j4t}$. The factor $e^{-3t}$ is the exponential envelope, and the negative exponent means that envelope decays toward zero as $t$ increases.
So the oscillation keeps going, but it is bounded by a shrinking envelope. That is the damping behavior you read from $\sigma<0$.

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{(3+j4)t}$, explain how the envelope behaves as $t$ increases.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the positive real part $\sigma=3$. That means the same factorization from the previous example will produce an envelope that expands as time increases.
Write $x(t)=e^{3t}e^{j4t}$. The factor $e^{3t}$ is the exponential envelope, and the positive exponent means that envelope grows without bound as $t$ increases.
So the oscillation keeps going, but it is bounded by an expanding envelope. That is the growth behavior you read from $\sigma>0$.

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{j4t}$, identify the envelope and explain why the amplitude stays constant.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the zero real part: this is the boundary case between decay and growth, so the envelope should be flat.
Rewrite the signal as $e^{0t}e^{j4t}$. The factor $e^{0t}$ is the envelope, and because $e^{0t}=1$, the amplitude stays constant.
So the signal only oscillates; it neither grows nor decays. That is the constant-amplitude behavior you read from $\sigma=0$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Determine whether and with what fundamental period the pure complex exponential $e^{j\omega t}$ repeats by enforcing $e^{j\omega(t+T)}=e^{j\omega t}$ and deriving $T_0=2\pi/|\omega|$ for $\omega\neq0$ within the generalized exponential signal family.

blocks.text: The first question is simple: when does the pure complex exponential repeat, and what does it mean for a shift to leave the signal unchanged? Start with the simplest nontrivial case, $x(t)=e^{jt}$, and treat periodicity as the existence of a nonzero shift $T$ that leaves the signal exactly the same.

For $e^{j\omega t}$, that definition becomes the test $e^{j\omega(t+T)}=e^{j\omega t}$. The goal is to see that this equality will collapse to a condition on the product $\omega T$, so the next steps can turn repetition into a period formula.
Keep the $\omega=0$ case in mind as the constant-signal exception; here, the main task is to recognize the repetition test and set up the algebra that will determine the period when $\omega\neq0$.

sections.section_title: Setting Up the Repetition Condition for $e^{j\omega t}$

example_content.example_prompt: Show that shifting $e^{j\omega t}$ by $T$ leads to the condition $e^{j\omega T}=1$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the repetition test from the previous step: a periodic signal must satisfy $x(t+T)=x(t)$ for some nonzero $T$. For $x(t)=e^{j\omega t}$, write the shifted signal and set it equal to the original signal.
Now cancel the common factor $e^{j\omega t}$ on both sides. What remains is the phase-only condition that must hold for repetition.

Because $e^{j\theta}=1$ exactly when $\theta$ is an integer multiple of $2\pi$, this is equivalent to $\omega T=2\pi k$ for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. The next step will use the smallest positive choice of $k$ to extract the fundamental period when $\omega>0$.

sections.section_title: Finding the Fundamental Period for Positive $\omega$

example_content.example_prompt: Find the fundamental period of $e^{j5t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the phase condition from the previous step: a repeated complex exponential must satisfy $\omega T=2\pi k$. Here $\omega=5$, so the smallest positive period comes from the smallest positive integer choice of $k$.
Choose $k=1$ to get the first positive repetition, then solve for $T$. This gives the fundamental period of the signal.
So $e^{j5t}$ repeats every $\frac{2\pi}{5}$ units of time. The period is positive, and this is the smallest shift that leaves the signal unchanged.

example_content.example_prompt: Find the fundamental period of $e^{-j5t}$ and express it using $|\omega|$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the same repetition test as before: a periodic complex exponential must satisfy $\omega T=2\pi k$. Here $\omega=-5$, so the sign changes the phase direction but the period still has to come out positive.
This gives the smallest positive shift directly. The negative sign in $\omega$ only changes which phase multiple you land on; it does not change the magnitude of the period.
So $e^{-j5t}$ repeats every $\frac{2\pi}{5}$ units of time. The minus sign does not change the fundamental period; writing the answer with $|\omega|$ keeps it explicitly positive.

example_content.example_prompt: Decide what happens when $\omega=0$ in $e^{j\omega t}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the endpoint of the same family. Set $\omega=0$ in $e^{j\omega t}$ and simplify; the signal becomes the constant $1$.
A constant signal does not change under any time shift, so the repetition test holds for every $T>0$.
So the nonzero-period formula $T_0=\frac{2\pi}{|\omega|}$ does not apply at $\omega=0$. The signal is periodic, but it has no unique fundamental period because every positive shift works.
